transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-04 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes (scheduled for 60)
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood Security PM); Carlos Ruiz (CISO, Epsilon), Aisha Mbaye (Cloud Architect), Tom Reynolds (Head of Platform), Mei Tan (Ops Sec)

Summary: Quick security review focused on encryption at rest/in-transit, BYOK/BYOK-HSM patterns, envelope encryption, rotation, and audit logs. Epsilon has a mix of cloud-hosted workloads and on-prem edge controllers; major concern is HSM integration and key custody for EU operations.

Topics: encryption at rest, HSM/BYOK, key rotation, audit trails, RBAC/SSO integration, network edge considerations

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — can you confirm names?
[00:06] Carlos: Yeah this is Carlos Ruiz from Epsilon, hi. Aisha here too.
[00:10] Aisha: Aisha, Cloud. Tom and Mei are on as well, can hear me.
[00:14] Jordan: Great. So purpose today is to walk our proposed key governance playbook for Redwood integrations and specifically the BYOM — BYOK flow and HSM options. I'll hand over to Maya to kick off with the architecture.
[00:25] Maya: Thanks Jordan. So high level — Redwood stores model state and inference payloads; we support envelope encryption using customer-managed keys in KMS or HSM-backed keys, so plaintext keys never land in our control plane. The flow is: client calls, we fetch encrypted model weights or cache keys, decrypt using envelope decryption with KMS, and then keep an in-memory key for KV cache — sorry, K-V cache — for inference.
[00:50] Mei: Sorry, can you hold — when you say in-memory key for KV cache, is that across warm restarts? We run edge controllers that sometimes are restarted nightly.
[00:58] Maya: Good question. Keys are cached for session lifetime and respect TTL. We avoid persisting unwrapped keys to disk. On restart, Redwood will re-request wrapped data keys from KMS/HSM and unwrap. That does add micro-latency on cold starts.
[01:14] Tom: How much latency are we talking about? Our edge controllers have 150ms SLO for control plane calls.
[01:20] Maya: Envelope unwrap is typically 20-80ms depending on HSM network hop and region. If the HSM is colocated, it's closer to 20–30ms. With a remote HSM across regions, add ~40–60ms. We can compensate with local cache warmers.
[01:35] Carlos: Hmm, so if we put HSM in our VPC in Norway, and Redwood hosted in eu-west, are we comfortable with the network hop?
[01:44] Liam: Network planning is key — we recommend HSM within same AZ or direct connect. For BYOK with external HSM (customer-managed), Redwood supports KMIP and PKCS#11 proxies. There are two patterns: 1) Redwood does envelope with wrapped data key via customer KMS API (we call unwrap); 2) Customer signs unwrap requests and we don't store unwrapped key at rest.
[02:09] Aisha: Can you repeat the two patterns — the terminology got clipped on the transcript earlier.
[02:13] Maya: Sure. Pattern A: Redwood requests a data key from customer-managed KMS/HSM — KMS returns a plaintext data key plus a wrapped version; Redwood uses wrapped for storage and plaintext in memory. Pattern B: Redwood receives only wrapped data keys; unwrap operations are proxied through customer KMS/HSM and Redwood does not hold unwrapped keys longer than necessary. Pattern B is tighter for custody.
[02:39] Tom: Pattern B is preferable for us. We want custody guarantees for keys that protect EU PII and industrial telemetry.
[02:46] Jordan: Quick interjection — for Pattern B we usually set up either an HSM in customer VPC with a relay endpoint or a cross-account KMS grant so Redwood can call unwrap with short-lived credentials. Both require network and IAM setup. We'll send an integration checklist.
[03:03] Mei: On rotation, what's the recommended cadence? Monthly? Quarterly? Our ops team prefers quarterly but security leans monthly for keys accessing sensitive telemetry.
[03:12] Liam: We recommend rotating data keys every 30–90 days depending on sensitivity. Envelope keys (master key / CMK) rotation is less frequent; typically annual rotation with automatic re-encryption strategies. The important bit: rotate the data keys and rewrap without having to re-encrypt blobs in storage by using key versioning metadata.
[03:33] Aisha: How is rewrap handled across many blobs and large model checkpoints? We have 10s of TBs of model artifacts in object storage.
[03:40] Maya: We use key-IDs and key version metadata so the wrapped key references the master key version. When a CMK rotates, you can either lazily rewrap on access, or kick a background rewrap job. For large artifacts like model checkpoints, we advise lazy rewrap on first access to avoid huge immediate compute. We'll include best-practice scripts in the playbook.
[03:58] Carlos: Auditability — we need immutable audit trails for unwrap calls, key usage, and rotation events for SOC 2. How detailed are Redwood's logs?
[04:07] Liam: Redwood produces audit logs that capture KMS unwrap/requests, timestamp, caller identity, request ID, and resource keys. For enterprise/private deployments you can ship logs to your SIEM or to a customer-managed S3 with retention rules. We sign logs and include HMAC for tamper-evidence in higher tiers.
[04:26] Aisha: Are logs stored in Redwood's control plane by default? Data residency concerns dictate logs for Norway stay in-region.
[04:33] Jordan: For Private deployments we can keep logs in your VPC. For Hosted, we support region pinning and can stream audit logs directly to your logging endpoint so they don't cross borders. We'll document the setup.
[04:46] Mei: SSO and RBAC — we'd like roles mapped to our IdP groups, not manual accounts.
[04:51] Maya: Redwood supports SAML and OIDC SSO. Role mapping can be automated via SAML assertions or SCIM provisioning. We also support granular RBAC: admin, deployer, auditor, readonly. We'll share a sample role matrix.
[05:06] Tom: If we provision cross-account unwrap permissions, how do we ensure least-privilege?
[05:10] Liam: Use fine-grained grants limited to unwrap/describe only and tied to time-limited tokens from STS or equivalent. We'll provide recommended IAM policy templates for AWS KMS as an example. For HSM, KMIP profiles can be scoped to operations.
[05:26] Carlos: A quick compliance question: does Redwood maintain SOC 2 Type II? We need that doc and the report.
[05:32] Jordan: Yes, Redwood is SOC 2 Type II; we'll share the attestation and relevant control mappings. Also, ISO 27001 is in process — we'll send the timeline.
[05:42] Aisha: Can you walk through a failure mode? For instance, if the customer KMS is unreachable, what happens to in-flight requests?
[05:48] Maya: By default, if unwrap fails, the request will error (we fail closed). We can set up a fallback model policy — e.g., route to a Redwood-hosted fallback CMK with a strict SLA and write-to-audit flag, but that requires contractual agreement. For many regulated customers, fail-closed is preferred.
[06:07] Tom: Fallback is risky for us. We need guaranteed control — fail-closed is our default. Is there a recommended retry/backoff and alerting pattern?
[06:16] Liam: Yes, we recommend exponential backoff for unwraps with jitter, a short-lived retry window (30s), and immediate alerting to Ops. We'll also surface metrics via the Console: unwrap success/failure rate, latency histograms, and a key usage dashboard.
[06:33] Carlos: Regarding HSM options — we run Thales and Gemalto appliances in some data centers. Compatibility concerns?
[06:40] Maya: We support PKCS#11 and KMIP gateways; customers often front their HSM with a gateway that offers a REST endpoint. For older appliances we recommend a middleware proxy that speaks KMIP. We'll include an HSM compatibility matrix in the pack.
[06:56] Aisha: Encryption in transit — we need TLS mutual auth for edge-to-Redwood control plane, and cert rotation. Does Redwood support mTLS?
[07:04] Jordan: Yes, mTLS is supported for Private deployments and can be configured for Dedicated. For Hosted APIs we use TLS 1.2+ and we support client certs via an optional mutual TLS layer.
[07:15] Mei: Is there support for hardware-protected keys on the inference nodes? For some of our latency-sensitive workloads we prefer on-node HSM or vTPM.
[07:23] Maya: We can support TPM-backed key storage for on-prem agents; for GPU inference nodes, HSM-backed keys are tricky due to PCI attach. The typical pattern is to keep keys in a nearby HSM and use short-lived session keys on the node. We'll explore the vTPM option for edge nodes in the follow-up.
[07:39] Tom: Any recommended quantization/serialization that impacts encryption? Checkpoint slicing?
[07:44] Maya: No difference functionally, but when slicing checkpoints you need to ensure each slice contains metadata with key-ID and version. That way rewraps are localized. We'll paste an example manifest in the artifacts.
[07:58] Carlos: Let's talk about proof-of-concept scope — we want Redwood to integrate with our KMS gateway in Norway, show envelope unwrap latency, and validate audit log delivery. Timeline expectation?
[08:07] Jordan: Typical POC is 4 weeks: week 1 integration and networking, week 2 unwrap testing and perf, week 3 log piping and access control, week 4 report and remediation.
[08:17] Aisha: We have a maintenance window week of 2025-12-22, is that a hard constraint?
[08:21] Jordan: We can work around that; we'll try to target integration before the window.
[08:25] Mei: For the POC, do you need admin-level access to our KMS? We prefer a least-priv principle.
[08:31] Liam: For initial test we need an unwrap role scoped for the test prefix and a temporary service account. We don't need full admin. We'll supply exact IAM policy.
[08:40] Tom: What about key rotation during the POC? We don't want a rotation to break testing.
[08:44] Maya: We'll use a static test key for POC and call out rotation as a separate test step.
[08:50] Jordan: Next steps recap: Jordan to send runbook and checklist; Maya to run perf baseline; Aisha to share KMS gateway endpoints and any region constraints; schedule follow-up for network/edge ops with Tom.
[08:59] Carlos: Sounds good. Anything else on certification or contractual controls?
[09:03] Jordan: We'll include suggested contract language for key custody, incident response, and data residency. Also, we can add a clause about fail-closed behavior for production.
[09:12] Aisha: One more quick thing — can Redwood provide example SIEM ingestion formats for our Splunk instance?
[09:17] Liam: Yes, we provide JSON and syslog samplers. We'll include sample ingestion templates.
[09:23] Mei: Thank you, that helps.
[09:26] Jordan: Great, we'll follow up with the artifacts. Appreciate everyone's time.
[09:30] (end of recording)

Notes on transcript quality: some product names may be garbled (e.g., 'K-V cash' for KV cache) and a few timestamps are approximate; speakers occasionally overlap which produced short crosstalk fragments.
